title: Before You Add More AI, Strengthen the Business Behind It
excerpt: AI becomes far more valuable when it understands the business it is being asked to support. Across Canada,…

featured_image.alt: A woman with short gray hair and glasses is shown on a blue background. Text reads: Jennifer Smart, Founder of Luxe AI Concierge. The CanadiansME logo appears in the lower left corner.

content_html:
AI becomes far more valuable when it understands the business it is being asked to support.

Across Canada, small businesses are being encouraged to adopt artificial intelligence at a remarkable pace.

AI can help draft emails, create content, summarize meetings, analyze information, support customer service and reduce repetitive administrative work. For founders managing multiple responsibilities, that potential is understandably appealing.

But before adding another AI tool, there is a more important question to ask:

Is the business behind the AI clear enough for the technology to support it well?

AI does not automatically understand how a business operates. It does not know which clients are the right fit, how a founder makes decisions, what the brand should sound like, where human judgment is essential or what a great client experience looks like.

It can only work with the context it has been given.

When that context is missing, the problem is often blamed on the technology. The AI sounds generic. Its recommendations feel disconnected from the business. Drafts require extensive editing. Team members receive different answers, and the founder spends more time correcting the output than benefiting from it.

The business may not need better prompts. It may need a stronger foundation.

AI exposes what has not yet been made clear

Many small businesses carry essential knowledge inside the founder’s head.

The founder knows which clients are a good match, how an inquiry should be handled and what needs to happen before work begins. They can recognize when an email sounds wrong, even if the company’s voice has never been formally defined. They understand the exceptions, preferences and unwritten standards that keep the business running.

This approach can work when the founder is personally involved in almost every decision. It becomes much harder to maintain as the business adds employees, contractors, systems or AI tools.

AI tends to expose these gaps quickly.

If a business has not clearly defined its process, AI may accelerate an inconsistent one. If important knowledge is scattered across inboxes, documents and individual team members, AI cannot reliably determine which information should guide its response. If the company’s communication standards exist only through instinct, AI will fill in the blanks with generic language.

That is why AI readiness is not simply a technology question. It is also a business infrastructure question.

Start with the work, not the tool

Before selecting an AI solution, founders should identify the business outcome they are trying to improve.

Is the goal to respond to inquiries more consistently? Reduce the time spent drafting routine communication? Improve onboarding? Organize internal knowledge? Help a team follow the same process?

Once the desired outcome is clear, the business can examine the workflow behind it.

For example, before using AI to support client onboarding, a company should be able to explain:

  1. What triggers the onboarding process?
  2. What information must be collected?
  3. Who is responsible for each step?
  4. What should the client receive and when?
  5. Which decisions require human approval?
  6. What does a successful onboarding experience look like?

If those answers are unclear, introducing AI may create speed without creating consistency.

A clear process gives the technology something dependable to support.

Give AI a business brain

AI performs better when it has access to organized, approved business context. This might include the company’s positioning, ideal client profile, services, decision rules, workflows, communication standards and examples of high quality work.

Together, this information acts like a business brain.

It helps AI understand not only what the company does, but how the company thinks and communicates.

This does not require a large corporate knowledge system. A small business can begin by documenting a few foundational areas:

Business clarity: What does the company do, who does it serve and what problems does it solve?

Workflow structure: How does important work move from one stage to the next?

Knowledge infrastructure: Where is the information required to complete that work stored?

Communication standards: How should the business sound in different situations?

Human review boundaries: Which outputs can assist the team, and which decisions must remain with a person?

These foundations make it easier to use AI consistently across different tools and team members.

They also remain valuable if the business changes platforms later.

Keep human judgment visible

Stronger AI does not reduce the importance of human leadership. It makes clear human leadership even more necessary.

A business should decide where AI can draft, organize, suggest or summarize, as well as where a person must review, approve or make the final decision.

Routine internal summaries may require only a quick accuracy check. Client communication involving conflict, pricing, commitments or sensitive information may need careful review. Strategic decisions should remain grounded in the founder’s experience, values and understanding of the business.

The goal is not to remove people from the work. It is to use AI where it can provide practical support while protecting the judgment, relationships and accountability that belong to humans.

Build clarity before complexity

Small businesses do not need to adopt every new AI tool to remain competitive. They need to understand where AI can create meaningful value and whether the business is prepared to support that use.

Before adding more technology, take one important workflow and document how it should operate. Gather the knowledge required to support it. Define the communication standards and identify the points where human review is necessary.

Then introduce AI with a clear purpose.

The businesses that gain the greatest value from AI may not be the ones using the most tools. They may be the ones that have taken the time to strengthen the knowledge, processes and judgment behind them.

Many businesses are using AI.

Far fewer are preparing the business behind it.

That preparation is where better results begin.

About Author

Jennifer Smart is the founder of Luxe AI Concierge, a Canadian human-led AI and businessinfrastructure consultancy. She helps founders organize the knowledge, workflows and communication standards behind their businesses so they can work with AI more clearly, consistently and confidently.

title: Closing the AI Action Gap: A Practical Starting Point for SMEs
excerpt: AI is changing the way businesses work. From improving customer experiences and analyzing information to streamlining workflows and…

featured_image.alt: Smiling man sitting on a stool in a warehouse, surrounded by cardboard boxes, with sunlight coming through nearby windows.

content_html:
AI is changing the way businesses work. From improving customer experiences and analyzing information to streamlining workflows and supporting better decisions, organizations are finding new ways to bring AI into their day-to-day operations.

But for many small and medium-sized businesses, the challenge is not understanding that AI matters. The challenge is figuring out where to start.

Many business leaders are asking the same practical questions: Where can AI create real value for our business? Which processes are worth exploring? How do we experiment without creating unnecessary risk? And how do we make progress when our teams are already balancing competing priorities?

These questions do not mean businesses are falling behind. They show that employers want to approach AI in a way that makes sense for their teams, customers, and operations.

The reality is that AI adoption is moving quickly, but confidence in using AI effectively has not kept pace. McKinsey’s 2025 Global AI Survey found that 88% of organizations regularly use AI across at least one business function, yet many companies are still working to move beyond experimentation and achieve meaningful business impact.

For SMEs, that transition can feel even more challenging. Without large technology teams or dedicated AI specialists, deciding where to focus time, resources, and attention is not always straightforward.

The first step is not having every answer. It is finding the right place to begin.

Want to understand where your business stands today? Take Riipen’s AI Readiness Self-Assessment to identify your current AI readiness and explore what type of AI-supported project could make sense for your organization.

[Take the AI Readiness Self-Assessment]

Moving from AI interest to AI action

Most businesses understand that AI will play an important role in the future of work. The challenge is turning that awareness into practical action.

Riipen’s State of the employer highlights this gap. While 76.2% of employers say AI skills are a priority, 42.4% had not yet considered student projects as part of their AI strategy.

This is what Riipen refers to as the AI Action Gap: the space between knowing AI matters and having a clear, practical way to begin.

For many SMEs, closing this gap does not start with a large technology transformation or a complex AI implementation. It starts with identifying one meaningful opportunity.

  • Where could AI help reduce repetitive work?
  • Where could it improve an existing process?
  • Where could a business test an idea, learn from the results, and decide what to do next?

A first AI project does not need to transform an entire organization. Often, the most valuable first step is a focused experiment that helps a business understand where AI can support its work, where human expertise remains essential, and what opportunities are worth exploring further.

AI adoption starts with confidence, not complexity

One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that businesses need advanced technical expertise to begin exploring its potential. In reality, many successful AI journeys start with something much simpler: understanding the business challenge first and identifying where AI could provide support.

For an SME, that might mean exploring ways to better understand customer feedback, improve internal processes, streamline repetitive tasks, support marketing efforts, or uncover new opportunities within existing workflows. The goal is not to introduce AI everywhere or chase the latest technology. It is to identify where AI can create meaningful value for the business and help teams work more effectively.

As Amanda Betts, Vice President of Growth at Riipen, shared during a recent discussion on AI adoption:

As Amanda Betts, Vice President of Growth at Riipen, shared during a recent discussion on AI adoption:

For employers looking to explore this topic further, Riipen’s webinar, The AI Action Gap, explores how businesses can move from uncertainty to action by focusing on practical experimentation, human judgment, and real-world applications of AI.

Why starting small can lead to bigger progress

When businesses think about AI, they often picture advanced automation, custom software, or complex technology projects. But for many SMEs, the most valuable first step is much more practical: starting with a focused business challenge, testing an idea, and learning what works before making larger investments.

This is where student-supported projects can create meaningful value. Students bring emerging skills, curiosity, and familiarity with new technologies, while employers bring the business context, customer understanding, and industry expertise needed to identify where AI can make a difference. Together, they create an opportunity to explore AI through real work, build confidence, and better understand where technology can support the business while keeping human judgment at the centre.

The result is more than a project deliverable. It is a clearer understanding of where AI can create value, what opportunities are worth exploring next, and how businesses can move forward with confidence.

Building a human-led approach to AI

The businesses that benefit most from AI will not necessarily be the ones using the most advanced tools. They will be the ones who understand where technology can support their work and where human expertise, experience, and judgment remain essential.

A human-led approach to AI adoption starts with the business challenge, not the technology. It means identifying where AI could create value, setting clear boundaries around how tools and information are used, and keeping people involved throughout the process. AI can help teams explore ideas, improve workflows, and support decision-making, but human judgment remains critical in determining what works, what needs to change, and what should come next.

The most effective way to build confidence with AI is through experimentation. Each project provides new insights into where technology can help, where additional support is needed, and how businesses can continue moving forward.

AI is not about replacing the expertise already inside a business. It is about creating new ways for people, technology, and emerging talent to work together to solve problems and create meaningful progress.

Taking the first step toward AI progress

Every SME is at a different stage of its AI journey. Some businesses are just beginning to explore what AI could mean for their organization, while others have already started experimenting but are unsure how to turn those early efforts into meaningful progress.

The challenge is that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to AI adoption. The right starting point depends on your business, your goals, your processes, and the opportunities where AI can create the most value.

Taking the time to understand your current readiness can help you identify where AI makes sense for your organization, where your team may need additional support, and what types of projects can help you move from curiosity to action.

Riipen’s AI Readiness Self-Assessment helps employers understand their current AI readiness and identify opportunities to explore AI through practical, human-led projects.

[Take the AI Readiness Self-Assessment]

For a deeper look at how SMEs can move from AI uncertainty to action, download Riipen’s white paper, “The AI Action Gap: The Human-in-the-Loop Employer.”

The white paper provides practical guidance on how businesses can approach AI without needing to start with complex technology projects. It explores how smaller experiments, student-supported projects, and a human-led approach can help employers identify where AI can support their work, build confidence, and make more informed decisions about what comes next.

Because successful AI adoption is not about doing everything at once. It is about finding the right opportunity, learning through experience, and creating a path forward that works for your business.

[Download the White Paper]

title: From AI Adoption to Real ROI: Turning Technology into Measurable Growth
excerpt: Artificial intelligence has evolved from a futuristic concept to a useful corporate tool. Small and medium-sized businesses throughout…

featured_image.alt: Hands typing on a laptop displaying “ROI” on the screen, with various digital data charts, bar graphs, and analytics icons overlaid, representing financial analysis and return on investment.

content_html:
Artificial intelligence has evolved from a futuristic concept to a useful corporate tool. Small and medium-sized businesses throughout Canada are experimenting with artificial intelligence to increase productivity, automate operations, and better understand their consumers. However, the biggest challenge for many SMEs is no longer whether they should employ AI, but how to turn these investments into measurable economic benefits. 

The CanadianSME Small Business Summit 2026, held this October at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, will bring together industry leaders, innovators, and entrepreneurs under the theme “Beyond AI: Building Intelligent, Resilient, and Human-Centered Canadian SMEs” to discuss the next stage of AI transformation: moving beyond adoption and making a real impact.

One of the key sessions, “From AI Adoption to Real ROI: Turning Technology into Measurable Growth,” will look at how SMEs can move beyond AI testing to develop strategies that deliver real results. 

Moving Beyond AI Experimentation 

Businesses have swiftly adopted AI-powered technologies for a variety of functions, including content development, customer support, data analysis, and automation. While new technologies present substantial prospects, many SMEs struggle to determine which solutions add true value. The difficulty is not just having access to AI tools; it is about understanding how they connect with business goals. 

To successfully adopt AI, firms must pose critical questions: 

  • What business challenge are we attempting to solve?
  • How will artificial intelligence (AI) increase productivity and consumer experience?
  • What measurable outcomes can we expect?
  • How can we incorporate AI into our existing workflows?

The panel will discuss why firms should shift from a tool-focused perspective to a strategy-driven approach in which technology supports certain goals. 

Turning AI Investments Into Business Results 

Every investment must help SMEs grow, improve efficiency, or become more competitive. When applied correctly, AI has the potential to add tremendous value. 

Businesses are increasingly embracing AI for: 

  • Reduce repetitive administrative tasks.
  • Improve operational efficiency.Improve customer engagement
  • Make quick, data-driven decisions.
  • Identify new market opportunities.
  • Using clever automation to support employees

However, attaining true ROI takes more than just adopting AI software. Companies must understand how technology fits into their operations and assess its impact using meaningful performance indicators. AI success is dependent on integrating innovation with measurable business benefits, whether it is cost reduction or revenue growth.

Avoiding the Challenge of “Tool Overload” 

With thousands of AI solutions on the market, many firms confront an additional challenge: selecting the correct tools. The rapid advancement of AI technology has resulted in a crowded market in which corporations can invest in various platforms without a defined strategy. This can result in high costs, unconnected systems, and limited results. 

The panel will discuss how SMEs can avoid “tool overload” by concentrating on: 

  • Choosing solutions depending on business needs.
  • Integrating AI into Existing Systems
  • Prioritizing scalability and long-term value
  • Ensuring that employees can efficiently use new technologies.

Rather than adopting every emerging tool, businesses can achieve more success by developing a targeted AI roadmap that aligns with their goals. 

Building Smarter Workflows With Human-Centered AI 

While AI may alter company operations, its greatest value is realized when technology collaborates with people. The future of AI-powered organizations is not about replacing human expertise, but about improving decision-making, creativity, and efficiency. 

Human-centred AI enables SMEs to combine the efficiency of automation with the strategic thinking, relationships, and creativity that underpin entrepreneurial activity. Businesses can improve internal operations and deliver superior customer experiences by equipping employees with better tools and information.

Learning From Real-World AI Success Stories 

The panel will include specialists who understand the practical aspects of AI application. Attendees will get a better grasp of how businesses can progress from AI curiosity to AI success by reviewing industry insights, frameworks, and case studies. 

Participants will discuss strategies for: 

  • Measuring AI Performance and ROI
  • Identifying High-impact AI Opportunities
  • Developing successful implementation plans
  • Creating competitive advantages with technology

The purpose is to provide SMEs with actionable knowledge that they can instantly utilize in their enterprises.

The Next Chapter of AI for Canadian SMEs 

AI adoption is just the beginning. Businesses that understand how to translate technology into meaningful outcomes will thrive in the next few years. The CanadianSME Small Business Summit 2026 will provide entrepreneurs and business leaders with the knowledge they need to navigate this next phase, in which AI is about more than simply innovation, but also growth, resilience, and long-term impact. 

As Canadian SMEs look to the future, the question is no longer whether they should use AI. The question is how they can strategically apply it to create smarter, stronger, and more human-centred enterprises.
